text: Measuring syndromes is only half the job. Something has to turn a lattice full of flipped and unflipped stabilizer outcomes into an actual decision about what correction to apply — and doing that fast enough to matter is itself an open engineering problem.

A decoder takes the full history of measured syndromes, every stabilizer's outcome across every round of extraction, and infers the most likely physical error chain that would explain exactly that pattern of defects. Once it has a hypothesis, it computes the correction — which physical qubits need which Pauli applied. This is a strictly harder problem than Lesson 10's simple lookup table, because the surface code's lattice has many stabilizers interacting over many rounds, not just 2 checked once.

The standard classical algorithm for this is minimum-weight perfect matching. Each defect becomes a node in a graph, and the decoder pairs up defects with each other, or with the lattice boundary for defects near the edge, such that the total cost of the chosen pairing is minimized — cost built to reflect how likely a given error chain actually is, with short, direct chains treated as more likely than long, convoluted ones. Perfect matching means every defect gets exactly one partner; minimum-weight means the decoder picks the pairing that costs the least across the whole lattice. This reduces decoding to a well-studied classical graph problem, reusing existing algorithms rather than inventing something from scratch — another example, like the CSS construction, of quantum error correction leaning on classical machinery.

Accuracy isn't the only requirement — speed matters just as much. Syndrome extraction runs continuously, round after round, for as long as a computation is running. If the decoder can't produce corrections at least as fast as new syndrome data arrives, a backlog builds up and error correction falls behind the physical qubits it's supposed to protect. Keeping decoding latency low enough at the lattice sizes genuinely useful fault-tolerant computation would require is an active area of engineering research, not a solved capability today.
Next lesson is this chapter's lab: computing qubit counts at new distances, and tracing through which stabilizers detect a specific error on the smallest practical lattice.
